power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .052 ", Sentence = "A study that yields p = .048 is classified as providing evidence for an effect; a study yielding p = .052 is classified as providing evidence against it."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: A Structured Framework for Cumulative Research Reporting in Psychology: Integrating Replication, Effect Sizes, and Meta-Analytic Evidence

author.affiliation:

								University of Málaga
								
									Málaga

text.text: R scripts and the simulated reference dataset are provided for full reproducibility.
continues to treat empirical studies as largely self-contained units evaluated primarily in terms of statistical significance and effect magnitude relative to a null hypothesis.
This approach, while familiar and institutionally entrenched, systematically undervalues the cumulative dimension of empirical inquiry.
The consequences of this fragmentation are well-documented.

Meta-analyses frequently reveal substantial heterogeneity in effect size estimates across studies examining ostensibly identical constructs (Borenstein et al., 2021; Hedges & Vevea, 1998), a pattern inconsistent with the assumption that published findings constitute a stable, coherent knowledge base.
text.formatted: Meta-analyses frequently reveal substantial heterogeneity in effect size estimates across studies examining ostensibly identical constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Borenstein et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hedges & Vevea, 1998)</ref>, a pattern inconsistent with the assumption that published findings constitute a stable, coherent knowledge base.

text.text: Replication failures, once characterized as isolated anomalies, have been reframed as predictable outcomes of a reporting culture that prioritizes novelty over precision and confirmatory significance over quantitative accumulation (Ioannidis, 2005; Simmons et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Replication failures, once characterized as isolated anomalies, have been reframed as predictable outcomes of a reporting culture that prioritizes novelty over precision and confirmatory significance over quantitative accumulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ioannidis, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Simmons et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Although reforms such as preregistration, open data mandates, and registered reports have made meaningful progress in addressing the structural incentives that sustain these problems, they have not directly addressed the fundamental issue of how individual studies relate their findings to prior evidence.
The present article proposes a structured framework, Cumulative Integrated Reporting (CIR), designed to address this gap.
The CIR framework specifies a set of reporting practices that operationalize the integration of new findings with existing evidence at the level of individual empirical papers.
Rather than treating meta-analysis as an activity conducted downstream from primary research, CIR embeds cumulative synthesis practices within the reporting of primary studies themselves.

In doing so, it reframes the epistemological function of the empirical paper: from a vehicle for announcing the presence or absence of an effect to a vehicle for refining and updating a quantitative estimate of an effect within a broader evidential context.
We develop the theoretical rationale for CIR in four steps.
First, we review the principal limitations of current reporting conventions in psychology and their consequences for cumulative knowledge generation.
Second, we describe the formal components of the CIR framework and the methodological procedures required to implement them.
Third, we provide a worked applied example illustrating how CIR operates in practice.
Fourth, we discuss the broader implications of CIR adoption for journal standards, educational practice, and the reconceptualization of replication as a continuous epistemic process.
The dominant model of reporting in psychology is organized around the logic of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST).

Under this model, a study's central contribution is defined by whether its results cross a predetermined significance threshold (conventionally p < .05), with effect size information typically reported as a supplement CIR FRAMEWORK to, rather than the focus of, inferential claims (Cohen, 1988; Cumming, 2014).
text.formatted: Under this model, a study's central contribution is defined by whether its results cross a predetermined significance threshold (conventionally p < .05), with effect size information typically reported as a supplement CIR FRAMEWORK to, rather than the focus of, inferential claims <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cumming, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The epistemological assumptions embedded in this model are not without merit, NHST provides a formal decision procedure for evaluating evidence against a specified null, but its application as the primary vehicle for knowledge synthesis has well-characterized limitations.
Chief among these limitations is the binary character of significance-based inferences.
A study that yields p = .048 is classified as providing evidence for an effect; a study yielding p = .052 is classified as providing evidence against it.

This categorization ignores the fundamental continuity of evidential strength and creates an illusory discontinuity at the threshold that has no direct bearing on effect magnitude or practical significance (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).
text.formatted: This categorization ignores the fundamental continuity of evidential strength and creates an illusory discontinuity at the threshold that has no direct bearing on effect magnitude or practical significance <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When multiple studies using the same threshold are interpreted in isolation, apparent contradictions (significant vs. nonsignificant) may reflect nothing more than sampling variability, yet they are typically reported and interpreted as substantive inconsistencies.
A related problem concerns the systematic underreporting of effect sizes in forms that facilitate cross-study integration.

Although effect size reporting has improved substantially since the American Psychological Association's (APA) 2001 publication manual revision (APA, 2010; Cumming et al., 2007), many studies continue to report effect sizes without the confidence intervals necessary to characterize their precision, and few studies situate their obtained effect sizes relative to the distribution of effects previously observed in the same research domain.
text.formatted: Although effect size reporting has improved substantially since the American Psychological Association's (APA) 2001 publication manual revision <ref type="bibr">(APA, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Cumming et al., 2007)</ref>, many studies continue to report effect sizes without the confidence intervals necessary to characterize their precision, and few studies situate their obtained effect sizes relative to the distribution of effects previously observed in the same research domain.

text.text: This absence of comparative context means that each study effectively begins the process of knowledge accumulation from scratch, rather than building incrementally on the quantitative foundation laid by prior work.

The replication crisis of the 2010s catalyzed a substantial reformulation of how scientific replication should be conceptualized and evaluated (Open Science Collaboration, 2015; Shrout & Rodgers, 2018).
text.formatted: The replication crisis of the 2010s catalyzed a substantial reformulation of how scientific replication should be conceptualized and evaluated <ref type="bibr">(Open Science Collaboration, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Shrout & Rodgers, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The traditional model treated replication as a binary verdict: a study either replicates (significant result in the same direction) or fails to replicate (non-significant or opposing result).
This framing has been extensively critiqued on both statistical and epistemological grounds (LeBel et al., 2018; Maxwell et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This framing has been extensively critiqued on both statistical and epistemological grounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(LeBel et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Maxwell et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Effect sizes vary across replications for numerous legitimate reasons, sampling variability, moderator differences, implementation fidelity, population heterogeneity, and a single failed replication no more falsifies a phenomenon than a single successful replication confirms it.
An alternative framework treats replication as a process of iterative effect size estimation (Cumming, 2012; Lakens & Etz, 2017).
text.formatted: An alternative framework treats replication as a process of iterative effect size estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cumming, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lakens & Etz, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Under this model, each new study contributes a data point to an evolving distribution of effect size estimates, and the scientific community's confidence in the existence and magnitude of an effect grows as this distribution becomes more precise and stable.
This model is statistically natural, it corresponds to the logic of meta-analysis, but it has not been operationalized at the level of primary reporting.
CIR is designed to bridge this gap by making iterative estimation a standard component of individual study reports.
The epistemological foundation most naturally suited to cumulative reporting is Bayesian inference (Dienes, 2016; Kruschke, 2014; Rouder et al., 2009).
text.formatted: The epistemological foundation most naturally suited to cumulative reporting is Bayesian inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dienes, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kruschke, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rouder et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: From a Bayesian perspective, scientific evidence accumulates through the successive updating of prior probability distributions in light of new data.

Prior distributions encode existing knowledge about a parameter of interest, in the present context, an effect size, and the CIR FRAMEWORK posterior distribution resulting from Bayesian updating represents the revised state of knowledge after incorporating new evidence.
This framework makes explicit the dependence of inference on prior knowledge, which is precisely what isolated reporting fails to acknowledge.
The CIR framework does not require researchers to conduct full Bayesian analyses, though it is entirely compatible with such approaches (Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018).
text.formatted: The CIR framework does not require researchers to conduct full Bayesian analyses, though it is entirely compatible with such approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Etz & Vandekerckhove, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, it requires researchers to characterize the empirical distribution of effect sizes from prior studies as a reference distribution against which their obtained effect size can be evaluated.

This is conceptually analogous to constructing an empirical prior, though it can be implemented through frequentist meta-analytic procedures, weighted mean estimation, heterogeneity assessment, prediction interval construction, that are already familiar to most researchers in psychology.
The CIR framework consists of four formal components, each corresponding to a discrete reporting requirement that supplements standard elements of primary research reports.

These components are designed to be modular, each can be implemented independently, though their combined use provides maximal cumulative benefit, and methodologically tractable within existing reporting conventions.
The first component of CIR formalizes the reporting of effect sizes alongside measures of their precision.
While effect size reporting is now nominally standard in psychology (APA, 2020), its implementation remains inconsistent.

CIR requires the reporting of (a) an appropriately chosen effect size metric (e.g., Cohen's d, Hedges' g, CIR FRAMEWORK Pearson's r, odds ratio) selected on the basis of the study design and measurement scales; (b) a 95% confidence interval reflecting sampling uncertainty in the estimate; and (c) where applicable, a bias-corrected variant of the effect size (e.g., Hedges' g rather than Cohen's d; omega-squared rather than eta-squared) to reduce overestimation in small samples.
The selection of the effect size metric should be explicitly justified with reference to the study design.
For between-subjects designs comparing two independent groups, standardized mean differences such as Cohen's d or Hedges' g are appropriate (Lakens, 2013).
text.formatted: For between-subjects designs comparing two independent groups, standardized mean differences such as Cohen's d or Hedges' g are appropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lakens, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: For correlational designs, Pearson's r or its variants provide a natural metric.

For pretest-posttest control group designs, the use of a pooled pretest standard deviation in the denominator of the standardized mean difference is recommended to avoid conflation of the treatment effect with within-group change variance (Morris, 2008; Viechtbauer, 2010).
text.formatted: For pretest-posttest control group designs, the use of a pooled pretest standard deviation in the denominator of the standardized mean difference is recommended to avoid conflation of the treatment effect with within-group change variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Morris, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: For more complex designs involving multiple factors or covariates, partial effect sizes (partial eta-squared, partial omega-squared) should be reported alongside their marginal counterparts.
Precision estimates should go beyond point confidence intervals to include prediction intervals where meta-analytic context permits.

A 95% prediction interval, derived from a random-effects meta-analytic model, specifies the range within which a future study's effect size would be expected to fall with 95% probability, given the heterogeneity of the existing evidence base.
Prediction intervals are systematically wider than confidence intervals around the mean effect and provide a more honest representation of cross-study variability (Riley et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Prediction intervals are systematically wider than confidence intervals around the mean effect and provide a more honest representation of cross-study variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Riley et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The second component requires authors to situate their obtained effect size within the distribution of effect sizes from prior studies addressing the same or closely related Where a relevant published meta-analysis exists, its summary effect size and heterogeneity estimates (I² , tau, prediction interval) should be reported as the primary reference distribution.
Where no meta-analysis exists, authors should compile a summary table of available primary study estimates.

The obtained effect size should then be formally compared with this reference distribution using two metrics: (a) the z-score of the obtained estimate relative to the meta-analytic mean and standard error, providing a test of whether the new estimate is consistent with the existing distribution; and (b) the percentile rank of the obtained estimate within the empirical distribution, providing an intuitive characterization of its relative magnitude.

Effect sizes that fall within one standard deviation of the meta-analytic mean can be interpreted as broadly consistent with prior evidence; those falling beyond two standard deviations warrant more detailed examination of potential moderating factors.
The third component operationalizes the Bayesian logic of evidence updating in a form that is accessible to researchers without advanced training in Bayesian computation.

Specifically, CIR requires authors to compute and report a meta-analytic updated CIR FRAMEWORK estimate that combines the existing evidence base with their new result using standard inverse-variance weighting procedures.
The updated meta-analytic mean is computed as: where θi is the effect size estimate from each study i (including the new study), and wi = 1/vi is the inverse of the corresponding variance estimate.

Under a fixed-effects model, vi is the within-study sampling variance; under a random-effects model (recommended when heterogeneity is plausible), vi includes an additional between-study variance component (τ² ) estimated via restricted maximum likelihood (Viechtbauer, 2005).
text.formatted: Under a fixed-effects model, vi is the within-study sampling variance; under a random-effects model (recommended when heterogeneity is plausible), vi includes an additional between-study variance component (τ² ) estimated via restricted maximum likelihood <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Viechtbauer, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Authors should report the updated mean, its 95% confidence interval, the heterogeneity statistic I² , and Cochran's Q with its associated p-value, using established meta-analytic software such as the metafor package in R (Viechtbauer, 2010) or Comprehensive Meta-Analysis.
text.formatted: Authors should report the updated mean, its 95% confidence interval, the heterogeneity statistic I² , and Cochran's Q with its associated p-value, using established meta-analytic software such as the metafor package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref> or Comprehensive Meta-Analysis.

text.text: This updated estimate constitutes the primary contribution of the CIRcompliant study to the cumulative literature.

By formally combining new evidence with existing evidence, it advances the research area's quantitative knowledge base in a manner that can be directly incorporated by future researchers implementing the same procedure.
The fourth component addresses the well-established challenge of cross-study heterogeneity in psychological effect size estimates.

Even when studies nominally examine identical constructs, they differ along numerous dimensions, sample characteristics, operationalizations of key variables, study context, measurement instruments, design features, that may moderate the magnitude of observed effects.

CIR CIR FRAMEWORK requires authors to explicitly document the features of their study that are most likely to function as moderators and to situate these features within the landscape of moderators characterizing the existing evidence base.

Documentation of potential moderators should be organized around four categories: (a) sample characteristics (e.g., age range, clinical status, cultural context, gender composition); (b) measurement operationalizations (e.g., specific scales or instruments, response formats, construct breadth); (c) design features (e.g., cross-sectional vs. longitudinal, lab vs. field, presence and type of control condition); and (d) procedural features (e.g., manipulations, timing of measurement, contextual factors).

Authors should explicitly compare their study's profile on these dimensions with the profile of studies included in the reference meta-analysis, highlighting dimensions on which their study is novel or divergent.

Where sufficient studies exist and appropriate data are available, authors are encouraged to conduct a priori moderation analyses using meta-regression procedures, testing whether the moderators they have identified significantly predict heterogeneity in the effect size distribution.

The goal is not to eliminate heterogeneity, which often reflects genuine contextual boundary conditions of psychological phenomena, but to characterize it with sufficient precision to support theoretical interpretation and to guide the design of future studies.
To illustrate the CIR framework in practice, we present a worked example using the association between emotional regulation and perceived stress.

This relationship represents an area of active empirical investigation with a sufficient accumulation of CIR FRAMEWORK primary studies to permit the construction of a meaningful reference distribution, making it a suitable candidate for CIR demonstration.

Suppose a researcher has conducted a cross-sectional survey study (N = 180) examining the relationship between cognitive reappraisal (a facet of emotional regulation measured with the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire; Gross & John, 2003) and perceived stress (measured with the Perceived Stress Scale; Cohen et al., 1983) in a sample of university students.
text.formatted: Suppose a researcher has conducted a cross-sectional survey study (N = 180) examining the relationship between cognitive reappraisal (a facet of emotional regulation measured with the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gross & John, 2003)</ref> and perceived stress (measured with the Perceived Stress Scale; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cohen et al., 1983)</ref> in a sample of university students.

text.text: The observed Pearson correlation is r = -.34 (95% CI [-.47, -.19]), indicating a moderate negative association: higher cognitive reappraisal is associated with lower perceived stress.

Under conventional reporting practices, this finding would typically be situated within a narrative literature review citing several prior studies, evaluated against the null hypothesis of r = 0, and interpreted through Cohen's (1988) conventional benchmarks (small: .10; medium: .30; large: .50).
text.formatted: Under conventional reporting practices, this finding would typically be situated within a narrative literature review citing several prior studies, evaluated against the null hypothesis of r = 0, and interpreted through <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cohen's (1988)</ref> conventional benchmarks (small: .10; medium: .30; large: .50).

text.text: The CIR framework requires a substantially more structured treatment.

A systematic search of the literature (databases: PsycINFO, Web of Science, MEDLINE; search terms: "emotional regulation" AND "perceived stress", "cognitive reappraisal" AND "stress"; date range: 2000-2024) yields N = 28 eligible primary studies reporting Pearson's r (or convertible statistics) for the association between cognitive reappraisal and perceived stress in non-clinical adult samples.

The weighted mean effect size across these studies, computed under a random-effects model using restricted maximum likelihood estimation, is r = -.31 (95% CI [-.37, -.25]), with substantial CIR FRAMEWORK heterogeneity (I² = 72.4%, τ = .11, 95% prediction interval [-.52, -.09]).

This reference distribution establishes that the researcher's obtained estimate of r = -.34 is consistent with the existing evidence base: it falls within 0.27 standard errors of the meta-analytic mean (z = 0.27, ns) and at approximately the 57th percentile of the empirical distribution.
The observed effect size is thus neither anomalously large nor anomalously small; it represents a plausible realization from the existing distribution of estimates.

Adding the new study to the existing evidence base and recomputing the randomeffects meta-analytic estimate yields an updated weighted mean of r updated = -.31 (95% CI [-.37, -.26]), with marginal changes to the heterogeneity estimates (I² updated = 71.8%, τupdated = .11).

The new study's contribution is primarily to increase the precision of the estimate (slightly narrower confidence interval) rather than to substantially shift its central tendency, which is the expected result when a new study yields an effect consistent with the prior distribution and the existing evidence base is already reasonably large.

This illustrates an important implication of the CIR framework: the contribution of a single study to cumulative knowledge is not primarily determined by whether it achieves statistical significance, but by the precision and accuracy of its effect size estimate and the degree to which it extends or challenges the existing distribution.

A well-powered study that yields a precise but unremarkable effect size estimate may contribute more to cumulative knowledge than a low-powered study that achieves significance through sampling variability.

CIR FRAMEWORK Relative to the reference distribution, the illustrative study is characterized by a relatively young, academically selected sample (university students, mean age 21 years), measurement of a specific facet of emotional regulation (cognitive reappraisal) rather than a composite emotional regulation index, and a cross-sectional design.
These features align with the modal study in the reference distribution, which may partly account for the consistency of the obtained estimate with the meta-analytic mean.

A subgroup analysis within the existing distribution indicates that studies using composite emotional regulation measures (vs. cognitive reappraisal specifically) yield somewhat smaller effects (r = -.27 vs. r = -.34; Qbetween = 4.31, p = .038), suggesting that cognitive reappraisal is among the more strongly stress-relevant components of the broader emotional regulation construct.

This moderation analysis, which becomes visible only through the structured comparative approach mandated by CIR, has direct implications for theoretical refinement and the design of future studies targeting emotional regulation as a mechanism for stress reduction interventions.
The CIR framework proposed here represents a reorientation of the epistemic function of the primary empirical paper in psychology.
Under the conventional model, the primary paper serves as the unit of scientific knowledge: a self-contained report of a study that either confirms or disconfirms a hypothesis.

Under the CIR model, the primary paper serves as a contribution to a running accumulation of quantitative evidence, a single data point in an iteratively refined effect size distribution, whose value is partly a function of how it relates to the estimates that preceded it. training.
Several practical resources support this pedagogical reorientation.
The metafor package in R (Viechtbauer, 2010) provides a comprehensive and freely available platform for conducting the meta-analytic calculations required by CIR.

text.text: Effect size calculators and converters (e.g., Lakens, 2013) facilitate the translation of reported statistics into common metrics.
text.formatted: Effect size calculators and converters (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lakens, 2013)</ref> facilitate the translation of reported statistics into common metrics.

text.text: The growing availability of meta-analytic databases and living systematic reviews in several domains of psychology substantially reduces the search burden associated with constructing reference distributions.
Several limitations of the CIR framework merit acknowledgment.
First, its implementation requires the existence of a sufficient prior literature from which to construct a meaningful reference distribution.

In genuinely novel research areas where fewer than five or ten prior studies exist, the reference distribution will be too imprecise to support robust comparative inference, and Components 2 and 3 of CIR can be implemented only in attenuated form.
Second, the quality of the CIR-generated cumulative estimates is contingent on the quality of the underlying primary literature.
A reference distribution constructed from studies with consistently small samples, selective reporting, or inadequate construct operationalization will yield biased estimates that CIR cannot correct.
CIR is best understood as a reporting framework that makes the evidential status of effect size estimates more transparent, not as a mechanism for detecting or correcting publication bias.

text.text: What is distinctive about the present moment is the convergence of methodological tools, open science infrastructure, and institutional will to implement change.

The CIR framework is offered as a contribution to this moment, a practical bridge between the reformist aspirations of the replication movement and the day-to-day reporting practices of empirical researchers committed to advancing a genuinely cumulative science of human behavior.

Implementation of CIR at scale requires the incorporation of its components into journal reporting guidelines.

Many journals in psychology have already adopted enhanced reporting standards (e.g., Journal Article Reporting Standards; APA, 2020), and CIR can be understood as a natural extension of these standards to address cumulative integration specifically.

We recommend that journals adopt CIR as a recommended reporting supplement for empirical papers, requiring authors to include (a) an effect size reporting table specifying the chosen metric, point estimate, and 95% confidence interval; (b) a prior evidence summary section presenting the reference distribution with metaanalytic statistics; (c) an updated evidence table reporting the result of incorporating the new study into the existing meta-analytic estimate; and (d) a moderator documentation table characterizing the study's profile on key design and sample dimensions.
The additional reporting burden imposed by these requirements varies as a function of the maturity of the relevant literature.
In well-developed research domains where published meta-analyses already exist, Components 2 and 3 require only the retrieval and documentation of available meta-analytic statistics.
In less developed domains, authors will need to conduct focused literature searches and compute reference distributions from primary studies.
While this represents a meaningful additional investment, it is one that is already implicitly required by rigorous scholarship, the CIR framework simply makes it explicit and structured.
The CIR framework offers a reconceptualization of replication that moves beyond the binary pass/fail model that has dominated replication crisis discourse.
Within the CIR framework, replication is not a discrete event with a binary outcome but a continuous process of effect size estimation that unfolds across the accumulation of studies.

A study that yields an effect size within the prediction interval of the existing meta-analytic distribution constitutes a successful replication in a meaningful statistical sense, regardless of whether it achieves conventional significance; a study that falls outside the prediction interval constitutes prima facie evidence of a boundary condition or moderating factor, warranting investigation rather than a verdict of failure.

This framing transforms the interpretation of replication results from a rhetorical contest, did Study B replicate Study A?, to a methodological inquiry: what does Study B's effect size estimate reveal about the true distribution of effects across contexts, samples, and operationalizations?

It also suggests a principled basis for designing replication studies: rather than targeting a specific prior study, replications should be designed to improve the precision of the reference distribution or to test the influence of a specific moderator.
The CIR framework has direct implications for how quantitative methods and research design are taught in psychology graduate programs.

Current training typically emphasizes the design and analysis of individual studies, with meta-analysis taught as a specialized technique for synthesizing completed literatures rather than as a framework that should inform the conduct and reporting of primary studies.

CIR implies a need to integrate meta-analytic thinking, including the construction of reference distributions, the calculation of updated estimates and the analysis of heterogeneity, into core methods

This comparative contextualization is the core innovation of the CIR approach and is what most fundamentally distinguishes CIR-compliant reports from conventional empirical papers.
Implementation of this component requires a focused literature search aimed at identifying existing studies or meta-analyses that have estimated the same or comparable construct relationship.

Authors should document the search process with sufficient transparency to permit evaluation of its comprehensiveness (e.g., databases searched, search terms, date range, inclusion and exclusion criteria).

text.text: Third, the operationalization of heterogeneity and moderator analysis in Component 4 requires judgments about construct equivalence across studies that are not CIR FRAMEWORK straightforwardly algorithmic.
Researchers must exercise judgment in determining whether studies examining nominally identical constructs are sufficiently comparable to warrant inclusion in the same reference distribution.
We recommend that authors document and justify their inclusion and exclusion decisions explicitly.
Future research should examine the empirical impact of CIR implementation on the coherence and cumulativeness of published literatures in psychology.
Simulation studies comparing the rate of knowledge accumulation under CIR-compliant and conventional reporting conditions would provide valuable evidence regarding the framework's efficacy.

Extensions of the CIR framework to experimental designs involving causal inference, multilevel data structures, and Bayesian estimation procedures would broaden its applicability across the full methodological diversity of psychological research.

Conclusion The CIR framework proposed in this article represents a structured response to one of the most persistent epistemological challenges in psychological science: the gap between what individual studies can establish in isolation and what the field requires to generate stable, generalizable, and practically applicable knowledge.

By embedding meta-analytic synthesis practices within primary empirical reporting, CIR transforms the individual study from an endpoint into a waypoint, a contribution to an iteratively refined evidential process that is larger than any single investigation.

The four components of CI, effect size reporting with precision estimates, systematic comparison with prior evidence, evidence updating through meta-analytic integration, and moderator documentation, are individually tractable and collectively sufficient to substantially improve the cumulativeness of psychological reporting.

Their implementation requires neither CIR FRAMEWORK wholesale methodological reform nor specialized training beyond the meta-analytic competencies that should already be part of the quantitative repertoire of publishing researchers.
